notes.1a: (i) Many candidates correctly drew on test-tube B a line level with the liquid in test-tube A and a layer indicating the level of sediment at the bottom and a label to the sediment.
notes.1aii: Many candidates were able to describe correctly how the graph paper scale was used by stating that they would count the number of squares between the top of the sediment and the bottom of the test-tube.
notes.1iii: Many candidates correctly stated that measuring the height of the sediment would be done for at least four regular time intervals.
notes.1iv: The majority of candidates organised their results clearly by presenting a ruled table. The stronger candidates included the heading ‘pH’ and the heading ‘height of sediment (mm)’. The majority of responses gained credit for recording the heights of sediment at each time interval and for each pH. Some candidates recorded pH3 or pH4 as the greatest height of sediment. The stronger responses recorded the heights as whole numbers.
notes.1v: Some candidates correctly completed Table 1.2 by recording the height of the sediment at each time interval for BU. Some candidates correctly estimated the pH of BU according to their results.
notes.1vvi: A few candidates suggested using at least five pH values to modify the procedure so as to obtain a more accurate estimate of the pH for BU followed by a comparison of their results with the results for the known pH values.
notes.1vii: A few candidates suggested correctly that at the pH where the greatest sedimentation occurred, yeast cells were more attracted towards each other causing the yeast cells to stick together and drop to the bottom of the test-tube.
notes.1viii: Some candidates correctly stated that a significant source of error was the difficulty of determining the boundary of the sediment when measuring the height of the sediment.
notes.1b: (i) Most candidates correctly used the headings given in the table to correctly label the x-axis (time/hours) and the y-axis (number of yeast cells/arbitrary units cm–3). Some candidates labelled the incorrect axis or gave incomplete headings. The stronger candidates, for the x-axis, used a scale of 5.0 to 2cm and for the y-axis, used a scale of 200.0 to 2cm. Many candidates plotted the five points correctly and joined the points accurately.
notes.1bii: Most candidates showed on the graph how to find the number of yeast cells at 18hours and stated the correct answer according to their graph.
notes.2a: (i) Credit was awarded to candidates whose drawings did not include any cells or shading and used most of the space provided. The stronger candidates gained credit for carefully following the instructions and drawing the shaded area as shown in Fig. 2.1. Many candidates gained credit for drawing at least four layers of tissue and for showing the outline of the vascular tissue as a wavy line. Most candidates used a label line and label to correctly identify the xylem.
notes.2aii: Credit was awarded for drawings made up of continuous lines which joined up precisely and used most of the space provided. Many candidates were able to draw four adjacent cells from the tissue close to the epidermis, each cell touching at least two of the other cells, with double lines representing the walls. The most common error was to draw lines that did not meet up precisely. Many responses were credited for showing a cell which had at least three angular sides. Most candidates used a ruled label line and label to identify the cell wall of one cell.
notes.2b: (i) The majority of candidates measured the line X within a range, with units. Most answers showed the measurement of X (mm) multiplied by 1000 and divided by 13 and gave the answer to the correct degree of accuracy.
notes.2bii: A few candidates correctly stated that the eyepiece graticule could be used by counting the number of eyepiece graticule units equivalent to the length of the vascular bundle and referring to a calibration technique to determine the actual length of the vascular bundle.
notes.2c: The stronger candidates organised the table into three columns, with one column for features, one headed J1 and one headed Fig. 2.2. Many candidates listed at least three observable differences between J1 and Fig. 2.2, such as the vascular bundles are joined together in J1 and separated in Fig. 2.2.
notes.key_messages:
Candidates should be given the opportunity to experience a variety of practical work throughout the course,
in order to develop the skills that can be applied to the requirements of the examination.
Candidates should be familiar with looking at experiments and assessing the relative importance of errors in
measurement or in making observations so that they can judge which sources of error are most significant.
Making a slight error when adding set volumes of buffer to set volumes of yeast cell suspension would not
decrease the accuracy of the results as there are other sources of error which are more significant such as
the accuracy of measuring the height of the sediment.
notes.general_comments:
Many candidates demonstrated that they had a good understanding of the skills required and the majority of
candidates were familiar with the use of the microscope.
